n: Given to Martin Harris, likely in summer 1829, as he hesitated to mortgage his farm to pay for printing the Book of Mormon. Christ introduces himself as Alpha and Omega — the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet — the beginning and end of all things.

f.g: first and last letters of the Greek alphabet; Christ is the beginning and the end.

n: Christ has fully accomplished the Father’s will, including the Atonement, which gives him power to bring all things under his rule.

f.w: having accomplished and finished the will of him whose I am

n: He keeps all power, including power to destroy Satan’s works at the end and to judge everyone by their deeds on the great final day.

f.w: judging every man according to his works

n: A sobering principle: everyone must either repent or suffer. God is endless, and his law cannot be sidestepped.

f.w: every man must repent or suffer

n: God does not take back his judgments; sorrow awaits those found on his “left hand” at judgment — an image from Jesus’ parable of the sheep and goats.

f.g: grinding of teeth in anguish or regret.

n: A key clarification: scripture doesn’t say the torment has no end; it says “endless torment.” The Lord is about to explain the difference.
Likewise “eternal damnation” — such strong language was used to move people’s hearts toward repentance, for God’s glory.
The Lord will explain this mystery to Martin, as he would to his apostles.
He speaks to those chosen for this work, united as one, so they may enter his rest.
Here is the mystery: “Endless” is one of God’s names. So “endless punishment” means punishment given by the Endless God — describing its source and kind, not necessarily its duration.
“Eternal punishment” means God’s punishment, since Eternal is also his name.
The same applies to “endless punishment.” This insight shows that God’s punishments are real yet purposeful, not merely infinite for the sake of it.
So Martin is commanded to repent and keep the commandments he received through Joseph Smith.
Those commandments came by God’s almighty power.
Christ pleads again: repent, lest suffering come that is more severe, intense, and hard to bear than Martin can imagine.

f.g: his word, which has power to judge.

n: One of the most important verses on the Atonement: Christ himself suffered these things for everyone, so that we need not suffer if we repent.

f.w: I, God, have suffered these things for all

n: But those who won’t repent must suffer as he did. The Atonement is freely offered but must be accepted.

f.w: they must suffer even as I

n: In the only first-person account of Gethsemane in scripture, Christ describes trembling with pain, bleeding from every pore, suffering in body and spirit, and wishing he could avoid the bitter cup.
Yet, giving glory to the Father, he drank the cup and completed his work for all humankind.
Christ commands Martin again to repent and confess, reminding him that he had tasted a small portion of this suffering when the Spirit was withdrawn — likely after the loss of the 116 pages.

f.w: at the time I withdrew my Spirit

n: Martin should preach only repentance, and not share these deeper teachings with the world until the Lord sees fit.
People can’t yet handle “meat,” only “milk” — they must learn simple truths before deeper ones.

f.w: they cannot bear meat now, but milk they must receive

n: A tender invitation: learn of Christ, listen to his words, walk in the meekness of his Spirit, and you will find peace in him.

f.w: you shall have peace in me

n: Jesus Christ came by the Father’s will and does his will.

f.w: I came by the will of the Father

n: Martin must not covet another man’s wife or seek anyone’s life — echoing the Ten Commandments.

f.w: thou shalt not covet thy neighbor's wife

n: Martin must not covet even his own property, but give it freely to print the Book of Mormon. He later mortgaged his farm for $3,000 to pay the printer.

f.g: to cling selfishly to one’s own possessions when God asks for them.

n: The Book of Mormon goes first to the Gentiles and then to the Jews — including the Lamanites as a remnant of Israel — so they can believe and stop waiting for a Messiah who has already come.

f.w: my word to the Gentile, that soon it may go to the Jew

n: Martin should pray aloud as well as silently, both publicly and privately.

f.w: pray vocally as well as in thy heart

n: He should declare the good news everywhere he can, “upon the mountains” — a phrase from Isaiah about messengers of peace.
Do it humbly, trusting in the Lord, and without insulting those who insult you.

f.g: revile = to criticize abusively. Don’t answer insults with insults.

n: Don’t argue over “tenets” — disputed points of doctrine. Instead teach the basics: repentance, faith in Christ, and forgiveness through baptism and the Holy Ghost.

f.g: specific doctrines or beliefs, especially ones people debate.

f.w: by fire, yea, even the Holy Ghost

n: This great commandment will guide Martin’s daily life to the end.
If Martin ignores these counsels, he will bring misery, even ruin of himself and his property.
He must give part of his property, even part of his land, keeping only what his family needs.
Martin is to pay the debt he agreed to with the printer, E. B. Grandin, and free himself from the bondage of debt.

f.g: Egbert B. Grandin of Palmyra, who printed the first 5,000 copies of the Book of Mormon in 1830.

n: Martin should leave home to preach, returning to visit his family when he wishes.
He should speak boldly and joyfully, shouting “Hosanna” — a Hebrew cry meaning “save now,” used in praise.

f.g: Hebrew, “save, we pray”; a shout of praise.

n: Pray always and God will pour out his Spirit, a blessing worth more than all earthly treasure.

f.g: things that decay and pass away.

n: The Lord asks: can you read this without rejoicing?
Or will you keep wandering as a blind guide?
Or can you be humble and meek and act wisely? Come to me, your Savior. The revelation ends with an invitation, not a threat.
